title: MUSE: Resolving Manifold Misalignment in Visual Tokenization
one_liner: Split gradient routes in vision models so pixel clarity and semantic meaning stop fighting each other.
lead: When a model learns to turn images into tokens (compact number lists that capture what the image shows), it faces an impossible choice: focus on pixel perfection or semantic understanding. The paper shows this is not a hard limit but a design flaw—when you optimize both at once, their gradients (learning directions) point opposite ways. MUSE physically separates where structural clues update from where semantic clues update, letting them reinforce instead of wreck each other.

problem.h2: The impossible choice in visual tokenization
paras: A tokenizer is the bridge between raw pixels and understanding: it looks at an image and squashes it into a list of abstract tokens (shorthand concepts like 'red,' 'edge,' 'texture,' or 'face'). But a good tokenizer does two opposite jobs: it must preserve every pixel detail—so a decoder can paint the image back perfectly—and it must forget irrelevant junk and group similar concepts—so the tokens carry only what matters for understanding the image.

These two goals pull in opposite directions. When training tries to keep every pixel, it learns to store clutter. When training tries to generalize, it throws away subtle details. Naive joint optimization—letting both goals tug at the weights at once—creates destructive interference: the weight updates that help one goal undo the other, because a single set of weights cannot satisfy two opposing signals at once, leaving the model stuck in mediocrity.

callout.html: Trying to be both perfectly faithful to pixels and perfectly abstract creates conflicting gradient directions that cancel each other out.

panels.title: 1. Naive joint training
panels.caption: Both goals tug the weights in opposite ways each step.

panels.title: 2. Pixel goal wins
panels.caption: Weights shift to capture every pixel, blurring semantic groups.

panels.title: 3. Structure route
panels.caption: A separate path learns which tokens carry structure (layout, edges).

panels.title: 4. Routes split
panels.caption: Structural updates flow through the router; semantic through feature values.

panels.title: 5. Both goals win
panels.caption: Routes reinforce: structure guides where to place semantic detail.

steps.text: Within the model, separate the path that learns arrangement (which tokens go where) from the path that learns meaning (what each token means).
When training pushes to improve layout and edge clarity, send that learning signal only to the attention-routing logic, because these weights control which tokens interact.
When training pushes to improve what concepts are encoded, send that learning signal only to the feature-value storage, because these weights hold the actual token meanings.
Track how well the two subspaces (routing space and value space) agree on what features matter, and nudge them toward orthogonality.
Structure and meaning now learn independently; updates that refine one naturally inform the other instead of erasing it.

paras: Standard tokenizers pool all gradients into one bucket—every learning signal goes to every weight. MUSE creates two separate gradient channels within the Transformer (the core model architecture): one channel tunes how the model routes tokens through attention heads (which tokens interact), and the other tunes the feature values stored in each token (what each token means). By decoupling the paths, conflicts vanish.

hidden.h2: Topological orthogonality: how aligned are the two subspaces?
hidden.name: Subspace alignment angle
paras: Inside a Transformer model are two learned subspaces: one that decides routing (which tokens activate for which images) and one that decides values (what content each token stores). If these two subspaces are similar (highly aligned), updates in one collide with the other. If they are perpendicular (orthogonal), an update in one subspace does not touch the other—they work in completely independent directions, like north and east on a map.

The paper estimates this alignment by measuring the angle between principal directions in each subspace. When the angle is close to 90 degrees, the subspaces are orthogonal and interference stops. The paper uses this measurement to steer the model toward orthogonality during training, keeping the two paths independent.

heat.caption: Darker means more misalignment (higher angle loss); light means orthogonal subspaces.

reads.html: Two learned paths should not interfere: they should be orthogonal (perpendicular).
Topological orthogonality: the principal component directions of the routing subspace and feature-value subspace should span nearly disjoint directions in weight space.

mechanism.h2: How splitting routes stops the fight
paras: In a standard Transformer, all weight updates happen in one pool. If pixel-level training says 'move weight w by 0.1' and semantic training says 'move weight w by -0.15,' the model does both, cancelling out. MUSE creates a barrier: weights involved in deciding *which tokens to route* get updates only from structural training; weights involved in storing *what tokens contain* get updates only from semantic training.

Inside a Transformer, the attention mechanism (which token talks to which) is geometrically separate from the value storage (what each token remembers). MUSE exploits this: it dedicates routing updates to the query and key computations (which decide attention), and semantic updates to the value and output computations (which decide content). Because these two functions use disjoint sets of weights, their gradients no longer collide. The paper enforces orthogonality as a soft constraint, nudging the two subspaces apart if they drift together. The result: structural clarity and semantic abstraction grow simultaneously instead of fighting.

stages.s: Structural gradient routed to attention layer
Semantic gradient routed to value layer
Check subspace orthogonality; add penalty if misaligned
Both pixel clarity and semantic meaning improve, because neither path disrupts the other

math.h2: The orthogonality loss that keeps the paths separate
math.words: Minimize: standard_task_loss plus (penalty_strength multiplied by the squared misalignment angle between routing-subspace and value-subspace).
symbols: the main goal: reconstruct pixels and encode semantics
how strongly to enforce orthogonality (a dial you turn up or down)
the angle in degrees between the principal directions of routing subspace and value subspace
the set of weight directions involved in token routing
the set of weight directions involved in token values

worked.title: A tiny numeric example
lines: Suppose in a 4-weight model: routing path uses w1, w2; value path uses w3, w4.
Initial task loss: 2.50 (reconstruction and semantic goals equally unhappy).
Initial subspace angle: 45 degrees (significant overlap, so misaligned).
After one update: routes w1, w2 away from w3, w4; subspace angle now 88 degrees.
Penalty = 1.0 times (88)^2 = 7744 — wait, that is higher! So we clamp: once angle > 85 degrees, penalty drops to near zero.
Revised: angle = 87 degrees, penalty ≈ 0; L_total = 2.48 (task loss shrinks, misalignment no longer fights it).

math.note: By adding a term that punishes misalignment, training naturally carves out orthogonal subspaces where structural and semantic updates no longer collide.

bars.h2: Trade-off broken: now both goals win

charts.title: Standard tokenizer (joint training)
rows: Pixel reconstruction (lower error means the rebuilt image is closer to the original)
Generation quality (lower FID means samples look more like real images)
charts.note: Trying to do both means doing neither well, because conflicting gradients drag weights in opposite directions, cancelling improvements.

charts.title: MUSE (orthogonal routes)
rows: Pixel reconstruction (lower error means the rebuilt image is closer to the original)
Generation quality (lower FID means samples look more like real images)
charts.note: Splitting routes lets pixel clarity and semantic meaning both improve, because each type of gradient only touches the weights it is meant for, so no cancellation occurs. No more zero-sum game.

items.html: If the orthogonality constraint is too weak (lambda too small), the two paths gradually merge during training and interference returns. The dial must be tuned.

items.b: One goal still dominates if not equally weighted.
items.html: If the pixel-reconstruction loss is much larger numerically than the semantic loss, gradients in that direction will dwarf the other. Both objectives must contribute equally to the updates.

items.b: Routing path may overfit to noise.
items.html: Separating routing updates makes the attention heads more expressive; without gently steering them (weight decay or dropout), they can learn spurious routing patterns that fail on new images.

items.b: Done right: tune lambda and balance losses.
items.html: With careful loss weighting and a moderate orthogonality penalty, the two subspaces stay independent, because the penalty steers them apart, and both goals improve in parallel without interference.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple image encoder (a small Transformer that turns 8x8 images into 4 tokens, each a list of 8 numbers). Train it on a toy dataset (MNIST or tiny-ImageNet crops) with two goals: (1) a decoder must reconstruct the image pixel-perfectly, (2) a linear classifier must recognize the digit or category from the tokens alone. Train once with joint optimization (all gradients in one pool) and once with MUSE (gradients routed to separate subspaces via an orthogonality penalty term). Log pixel reconstruction error and classifier accuracy over 100 steps. Plot both curves for each method. MUSE should show both metrics improving together; joint training should show a see-saw.
demo.closing: The demo must make it visible that MUSE trades off less—both metrics improve simultaneously—proving that the two goals no longer fight, because decoupled gradient paths prevent cancellation.
